airport: Airports are large transportation hubs characterized by long, wide gray runways with bright white markings and clusters of large buildings. Unlike viaducts, which are elevated road structures, airports feature flat expanses with massive landing strips; unlike industrial areas, which are dominated by factory buildings, airports focus on aviation infrastructure; and unlike parking lots, which are filled with rows of cars, airports have large aprons with passenger boarding bridges.
bareland: Bareland consists of exposed soil or rock with a smooth texture and minimal vegetation, appearing in flat or gently sloping terrain. Unlike deserts, which have vast, continuous sand expanses, bareland often shows patches of dirt or gravel; compared to farmland, it lacks organized agricultural plots or crop rows; and unlike meadows, it lacks continuous grassy vegetation, appearing mostly as barren earth.
baseballfield: A baseball field is defined by its distinctive fan-shaped layout, featuring a brown or tan dirt infield, white base paths, and a green outfield. Unlike tennis courts, which are rectangular, baseball fields have a curved outfield boundary; compared to parking lots, they are recreational spaces without rows of cars; and unlike stadiums, which are enclosed by large structures, baseball fields are open playing areas.
beach: Beach areas are coastal strips of bright tan or white sand separating water from land, often with adjacent resort developments. Unlike bareland, beaches are strictly coastal and feature fine sand textures rather than inland dirt; compared to rivers, beaches are static landforms rather than flowing water bodies; and unlike resorts, beaches are natural shores without dense clustered buildings or pools.
bridge: Bridges are linear structures spanning water bodies or valleys, appearing as straight or curved paved roads connecting separate landmasses. Unlike viaducts, which are long, elevated highway segments crossing land, bridges specifically cross water features like rivers or ponds; compared to railways, bridges carry vehicular traffic rather than trains; and unlike ports, bridges are transit infrastructures rather than areas for docking ships.
center: Centers are urban core areas characterized by high-density building clusters, often containing commercial, cultural, and residential structures. Unlike sparse residential areas, centers have extremely high building density with little to no yards; compared to industrial zones, centers lack large warehouses or factories; and unlike railway stations, centers are broad urban districts rather than specific transit hub buildings.
church: Churches are identified by their distinct religious architecture, often featuring sharp spires, crosses, or pitched roofs, and usually stand isolated in neighborhoods. Unlike commercial buildings, churches have unique vertical structural features and are not purely rectangular; compared to schools, churches typically have smaller footprints and distinct religious symbols; and unlike resorts, they are places of worship rather than recreational facilities.
commercial: Commercial areas are filled with large, rectangular buildings with flat roofs, often surrounded by parking lots, located along main roads. Unlike industrial areas, commercial zones have retail buildings rather than large factories or storage tanks; compared to centers, commercial areas are less dense and more spread out; and unlike railway stations, commercial zones are retail districts rather than transit hubs.
denseresidential: Dense residential areas consist of tightly packed small buildings with uniform, repetitive roof patterns, creating a high-density spatial layout with minimal vegetation. Unlike medium residential areas, dense residential areas have smaller footprints and tighter spacing; compared to sparse residential areas, the structures are much closer together with almost no yards; and unlike commercial zones, these are purely residential without large retail buildings.
desert: Deserts are vast, continuous expanses of flat terrain covered with sand, exhibiting uniform light tan or yellow colors. Unlike bareland, which may be smaller patches of exposed earth, deserts are massive continuous sandy expanses; compared to meadows, deserts lack any green vegetation; and unlike farmland, deserts have no geometric field boundaries or irrigation systems.
farmland: Farmland consists of regular geometric plots of cultivated land with varying textures and colors, often showing crop rows or irrigation circles. Unlike meadows, which are natural continuous grass covers, farmland has distinct organized boundaries and planting patterns; compared to bareland, it has active vegetation or distinct soil treatment; and unlike forests, farmland lacks dense tree canopies, appearing as open fields.
forest: Forest areas are identified by a continuous, dense canopy of trees with a rough, mottled texture and dark green tones, often casting collective shadows. Unlike mountains, which have rocky peaks and steep slopes, forests are flat or hilly terrains covered entirely by trees; compared to farmland, forests lack regular geometric planting patterns and appear as natural, unstructured expanses; and unlike meadows, forests have dense, tall tree canopies rather than short grass.
industrial: Industrial areas contain large, rectangular factory buildings with metallic roofs, often accompanied by storage tanks or loading docks. Unlike commercial areas, industrial zones have massive footprint buildings designed for manufacturing rather than retail; compared to storage tank areas, industrial zones contain large warehouses rather than just cylindrical structures; and unlike railway stations, industrial areas are manufacturing hubs rather than passenger transit centers.
meadow: Meadows are expanses of open, natural grassy terrain with a smooth texture and light green color, lacking tree cover. Unlike farmland, meadows lack regular geometric boundaries or crop rows; compared to forests, meadows are entirely absent of tall trees, offering a flat visual profile; and unlike bareland, meadows have continuous grassy vegetation rather than exposed soil.
mediumresidential: Medium residential areas display a mix of single-family homes with moderate spacing, showing a balance between built structures and surrounding greenery or lawns. Unlike dense residential areas, which have tightly packed roofs, medium residential areas have larger yards and more visible vegetation between houses; compared to sparse residential areas, the housing density is higher with less undeveloped land; and unlike commercial zones, these are purely residential without large retail buildings.
mountain: Mountainous regions are characterized by rugged, elevated topography with steep slopes, rocky peaks, and intricate shadow patterns caused by the terrain. Unlike forests, which have a continuous tree canopy, mountains show exposed rock, snow, or sparse vegetation; compared to bareland, mountains have distinct elevation changes and complex ridges; and unlike rivers, mountains are solid landforms rather than flowing water bodies.
park: Parks are designated recreational areas featuring continuous manicured green lawns, scattered trees, and often winding pathways. Unlike meadows, which are natural grasslands, parks show intentional landscaping with planted trees and paths; compared to forests, parks have open grassy areas rather than dense, unbroken tree canopies; and unlike parking lots, parks are vegetated recreational spaces rather than paved surfaces for vehicles.
parking: Parking lots are large, flat, paved rectangular areas with visible grid-like rows of parked vehicles, often adjacent to commercial or residential zones. Unlike storage tank areas, which contain clustered circular structures, parking lots have rows of rectangular vehicles; compared to bridges, parking lots are flat stationary storage areas rather than linear transit structures; and unlike schools, they are purely paved spaces without playgrounds or large educational buildings.
pond: Ponds are small, natural or man-made water bodies enclosed by land, often appearing as dark blue or black irregular shapes. Unlike rivers, which are linear and flowing, ponds are compact and static; compared to beaches, ponds are inland water bodies rather than coastal sand shores; and unlike viaducts, ponds are natural water features rather than elevated road structures.
port: Ports are coastal water-land interfaces characterized by clustered ships, cranes, and linear docks, serving as hubs for maritime shipping. Unlike airports, which are aviation hubs with runways, ports feature docks and watercraft; compared to bridges, ports are stationary docking areas rather than transit structures crossing water; and unlike industrial zones, ports focus on maritime logistics rather than manufacturing buildings.
playground: Playgrounds are small recreational areas with distinct surface markings, such as geometric tracks or courts, often surrounded by green spaces or schools. Unlike baseball fields, which have a specific fan shape and dirt infield, playgrounds have various rectangular or circular sports markings; compared to parking lots, they are recreational spaces rather than vehicle storage; and unlike stadiums, playgrounds lack large surrounding spectator stands.
railwaystation: Railway stations are transit hubs characterized by linear clusters of train cars, long parallel platforms, and station buildings. Unlike airports, which have airplanes and runways, railway stations feature trains and tracks; compared to bridges, railway stations are wider transit hubs with buildings rather than narrow crossing structures; and unlike industrial areas, they are passenger or freight transit centers rather than manufacturing zones.
resort: Resorts are recreational areas featuring clusters of large buildings mixed with amenities like pools, golf courses, and landscaped gardens. Unlike beaches, which are natural sandy shores, resorts have built structures and recreational facilities; compared to centers, resorts are spread out with extensive greenery rather than dense urban cores; and unlike churches, resorts are leisure destinations rather than isolated religious structures.
river: Rivers are natural, flowing water bodies with sinuous, irregular curves that adapt to the topography, often surrounded by riparian vegetation. Unlike bridges, which are linear paved structures crossing water, rivers are the water bodies themselves; compared to ponds, rivers are long and flowing rather than compact and static; and unlike bareland, rivers are water features rather than exposed earth.
school: Schools are educational complexes characterized by large main buildings surrounded by green playgrounds, tracks, and parking lots. Unlike residential areas, schools have institutional buildings and sports facilities rather than houses; compared to parks, schools have prominent built structures and pavilions rather than just green spaces; and unlike parking lots, schools are educational campuses with buildings rather than just paved vehicle storage.
sparseresidential: Sparse residential areas are characterized by widely spaced individual houses surrounded by large expanses of natural or undeveloped land, showing very low housing density. Unlike medium residential areas, sparse residential areas have much larger distances between buildings; compared to bareland, they feature built structures rather than just exposed soil; and unlike farmland, they are residential zones rather than cultivated geometric fields.
square: Squares are urban open spaces with paved surfaces, often surrounded by buildings or roads, designed for public gatherings. Unlike playgrounds, which have sports markings, squares are flat paved areas without specific athletic court lines; compared to parking lots, squares lack rows of parked cars and are intended for pedestrian use; and unlike parks, squares are paved rather than covered with grass and trees.
stadium: Stadiums are large, enclosed structures featuring a massive central playing field surrounded by tiered seating, often with a distinctive oval or circular footprint. Unlike playgrounds, which are open and small, stadiums are massive enclosed structures; compared to baseball fields, stadiums have large surrounding spectator stands rather than just an open field; and unlike industrial areas, stadiums are sports venues rather than manufacturing buildings.
storagetanks: Storage tanks are circular, cylindrical structures with smooth surfaces and distinct shadows, often grouped closely together in industrial zones. Unlike parking lots, which are flat surfaces with rectangular vehicles, storage tanks are elevated 3D structures with circular footprints; compared to buildings, storage tanks have uniform, curved geometries rather than rectangular architectural forms; and unlike rivers, they are solid industrial structures rather than water bodies.
viaduct: Viaducts are long, elevated road structures supported by a series of arches or piers, crossing over valleys or urban areas. Unlike bridges, which typically cross water bodies, viaducts traverse land or urban infrastructure; compared to railways, viaducts carry vehicular traffic rather than trains; and unlike airports, viaducts are narrow transit lines rather than flat expanses with runways.
